title: Could you draw a familiar logo from memory?

sources.name: Blake, Nazarian & Castel (2015) — Original study abstract: memory and confidence for the Apple logo
UCLA — Report on the 2015 Apple-logo study and its undergraduate sample

practice: Try World Flags for another kind of visual question. Before choosing, notice which detail your answer depends on: a colour, a shape or its position.

sections.html:
A logo can feel familiar without every detail being easy to recall. Before looking, sketch a simple logo you know, or describe it in words. First note how sure you feel.

Then check the real design. Did a leaf turn the wrong way, or a small part disappear?
sections.title: Familiar does not mean every detail is stored

sections.html:
In a 2015 Apple-logo study, only one of 85 participants drew it correctly. Fewer than half recognised the correct design among similar versions.

UCLA identifies the sample as undergraduates. Participants overestimated their performance; overconfidence was lower when they judged their ability after drawing.

Those results describe this sample and task, not everyone’s memory.
sections.title: A familiar apple surprised the researchers

sections.html:
Recall means bringing something to mind without seeing it. Recognition means identifying it when shown. Familiarity is the feeling of having seen it before.

The researchers suggested people may overlook details they do not need. Frequent exposure need not mean close attention; that is a possible explanation, not proof of one cause.
sections.title: Knowing the look is not knowing every detail

sections.html:
Compare three things: parts, positions and directions. Ignore drawing neatness. Did you add anything, omit anything or flip a detail?

This small observation is not an intelligence test or a measure of your memory overall.
sections.title: Check one detail at a time

sections.html:
Before choosing a quiz answer, name one detail you are relying on: “the stripe order” is more specific than “it looks right”. Then check it.

Try recalling the answer later, or explore what happens after a wrong first guess.

Does feeling certain prove the details are right?

No. Confidence is how sure you feel; checking a reliable reference tests the details.
sections.title: Try the same pause with your next answer

description: A logo can feel familiar while its details stay fuzzy. Try a quick drawing challenge, then discover what an Apple-logo study found about confidence and memory.
